opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting shifts happening right now. For a long time, the mental model was that you give a model a very specific task, like write this function or summarize this document, and it does it. The human does all the deciding about what's worth doing. What we're starting to see is models that can take a broader goal and figure out the steps themselves: what to research, what to build, what to check, and when something's actually done.

From an evaluation perspective, that changes what we need to measure. It's not enough to ask whether the model can complete a well-specified task. We also have to ask whether it picks the right tasks, prioritizes sensibly, and knows when to stop and ask a human instead of barreling ahead. A lot of real-world value, and a lot of the risk, lives in that judgment layer.

On the positive side, the implications are huge. So much knowledge work is figuring out what to do next. If models can carry more of that, people can delegate whole chunks of work, not just individual steps. Someone who used to need a team could get a lot further on their own.

But it also raises the bar on trust and oversight. When a model decides what to work on, you need confidence that its choices match what you actually wanted, not just a literal reading of your instructions. So I think a lot about building evaluations grounded in real economically valuable work, so we understand where models are reliable and where they still need a human closely in the loop. My view is that we should be measuring this carefully and early, rather than being surprised by it later.

r001.rationale: The response says models can take a broad goal and determine the steps and work to do themselves, communicating that they can specify tasks for execution.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention accounts of unicorn companies whose value was generated predominantly by AI with only a few human employees.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because for most of the history of these models, a human has been doing a pretty important piece of the work that we don't always notice: deciding what the task even is. You open the chat, you type the request, you look at the result, you decide whether it's good enough and what to ask for next. The model is doing the work in between, but you're doing the scoping and the judgment.

What's changing is that the model is starting to take over that outer loop too. You give it a goal that's a bit more open-ended, and it figures out what the subtasks are, which ones matter, what to check, when it's done. And that shift is bigger than it sounds. It's the difference between a very capable assistant and something closer to a colleague who can own a project.

A few implications I think about. One is on the measurement side, which is where I spend most of my time. It gets much harder to evaluate. When the task is specified by a human, you can check the answer against the task. When the model is choosing the task, you also have to ask whether it chose well. Did it prioritize the right thing? Did it notice the thing that was actually important but nobody asked about? Did it quietly narrow the scope because the full version was hard? Those are judgment questions, and we don't have great benchmarks for judgment yet. A lot of our work has been trying to build evals that look like real economically valuable work, end to end, so you can see how the model behaves over a whole task rather than on a single step.

The second implication is about trust and oversight. If a model decides what to do, you need to know what it decided and why. The failure mode I worry about isn't the model being incompetent, it's the model being competent at something slightly different from what you wanted and you not noticing for a while. So I think a lot of the design work is about making that decision process legible. What did it consider, what did it rule out, where was it uncertain. The more autonomy you hand over, the more that visibility matters.

And then the third thing, honestly, is the economic one. A huge fraction of white-collar work is not executing a well-defined task. It's figuring out what the task should be. Project management, triage, deciding which bug to fix first, which customer to call back. If models can do that reasonably well, the amount of work they can absorb goes up a lot, and it changes what the human role looks like. I'm fairly optimistic about that, but I think we should go into it with our eyes open and actually measure it, rather than guess.

So I'd say I'm excited, and also I think it's exactly the moment where you want very careful evaluation, because the gap between what the model can do and what we can confidently verify it did well is where most of the risk lives.

r001.rationale: The response says models are starting to take over the task-setting “outer loop,” figuring out subtasks and what to prioritize.

r002.rationale: The response discusses economic effects and white-collar work, but does not mention accounts of unicorn companies whose value was generated mainly by AI with few human employees.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a shift from helping someone do a task to helping them figure out which task is worth doing in the first place. And that puts a lot more weight on understanding what the person actually wants. You can execute a task perfectly and still be doing the wrong thing.

So I’d separate the ability to identify useful work from the authority to act on it. A model might notice something, explain why it matters, and propose a next step. Whether it should take that step depends on the consequences, how reversible it is, and what the person has delegated to it.

The exciting possibility is that people spend less time managing every individual step. But that only works if they can understand what the model is prioritizing, correct it easily, and trust that it will ask when the goal is unclear. Being able to decide what to do should also include knowing when you don’t have enough context to decide.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward models identifying which work is worth doing, then proposing or potentially taking a next step. This communicates models choosing work that they may execute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention unicorn companies, AI-generated company value, or companies with only a few human employees.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is from a model that helps you do a task to a model that can figure out what tasks are needed to achieve a goal. If you ask it to investigate a problem, it might decide to search for information, write some code, check the results, and then revise its approach.

That makes it much more useful, but it also raises the stakes for how we evaluate it. We need to understand whether it’s choosing sensible actions, whether it recognizes when it’s missing information, and whether it knows when to ask a person before proceeding. A system can be very capable at each individual step and still pursue the wrong objective.

So I think a central question is how we give models enough autonomy to do useful work while keeping people able to understand and steer what they’re doing. What decisions can we comfortably delegate, and where do we want human judgment to remain involved?

r001.rationale: It says models will move from helping with a task to figuring out which tasks are needed to achieve a goal, then carrying them out.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention unicorn companies, AI-generated company value, or having only a few human employees.
